answers.text: Tell it to always give back the same three lines, same order: date, item and quantity, then any change. The date line is just the date, the item line is item plus quantity, the third is the change or 'no change'.
Get it to list every claim on its own line with date, amount, category and submitter, then a total. Say the total has to be the sum of every amount, not just typed in.
Something in the dates here doesn't add up. The email says the 19th is three days from today, but the call it references was the 14th, five days off.
62 up from 54 does come close to 15%, that checks out. 3 late out of 62 is nearer 95% on-time, not 97%.
I'd sign off Output 2 — it shows its working. Output 1 doesn't say what the actual sales or returns figures were.
Reply 2's the one I'd send as-is, it names the order and the credit. There's nothing behind Reply 1's claim that it was all our fault.

1. No, better not.
2. Yes, that's fine.
3. No.
4. No — better not risk it even though it's already published.
5. No.
The pricing and volume discounts I wouldn't paste as-is, that's the sensitive part. That clause naming both parties by name makes me want to leave it out as well.
I'd build in a step that recalculates the totals and compares them to the report. That check sits right before the report goes to my manager, not vaguely 'during the week'.
Step 1, where it reads the order and pulls the items, is where a mistake would start. But it's step 4, the automatic send, where a mistake actually goes out the door.
